# again - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/again/

## Expand description

`Again` is a wasm-compatible utility for retrying standard library [ Futures](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/future/trait.Future.html) with a

`Result` output typeA goal of any operation should be a successful outcome. This crate gives operations a better chance at achieving that.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#hello-world)Hello world

For simple cases, you can use the module level [ retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html) fn, which
will retry a task every second for 5 seconds with an exponential backoff.

`again::retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));`[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-retries)Conditional retries

By default, `again` will retry any failed `Future` if its `Result` output type is an `Err`.
You may not want to retry *every* kind of error. In those cases you may wish to use the [ retry_if](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_if.html) fn, which
accepts an additional argument to conditionally determine if the error
should be retried.

```
again::retry_if(
    || reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"),
    reqwest::Error::is_status,
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#retry-policies)Retry policies

Every application has different needs. The default retry behavior in `again`
likely will not suit all of them. You can define your own retry behavior
with a [ RetryPolicy](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html). A RetryPolicy can be configured with a fixed or exponential backoff,
jitter, and other common retry options. This objects may be reused
across operations. For more information see the

[docs.](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)

`RetryPolicy`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use again::RetryPolicy;
use std::time::Duration;
let policy = RetryPolicy::fixed(Duration::from_millis(100))
    .with_max_retries(10)
    .with_jitter(false);
policy.retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

For visibility on when operations fail and are retried, a `log::trace` message is emitted,
logging the `Debug` display of the error and the delay before the next attempt.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-features)wasm features

`again` supports [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/) targets i.e. `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which should make this
crate a good fit for most environments

Two cargo features exist to support various wasm runtimes: `wasm-bindgen` and `stdweb`.
To enable them add the following to your `Cargo.toml` file.

```
[dependencies]
again = { version = "xxx", features = ["wasm-bindgen"] }
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Retry](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)- Policy
- A template for configuring retry behavior

# again 0.1.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/again/latest

A goal of any operation should be a successful outcome. This crate gives operations a better chance at achieving that.

## 📦 install

In your Cargo.toml file, add the following under the `[dependencies]` heading

```
 = "0.1"
```
## 🤸usage

For very simple cases you can use the module level `retry` function
to retry a potentially fallible operation.

```
use Error;
async
```
You may not want to retry *every* kind of error. For preciseness you can be more explicit in which kinds of errors should be retried with the module level `retry_if` function.

```
use Error;
async
```
You can also customize retry behavior to suit your applications needs
with a configurable and reusable `RetryPolicy`.

```
use Error;
use Duration;
use RetryPolicy;
async
```
See the [docs](http://docs.rs/again) for more examples.

Doug Tangren (softprops) 2020

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/rand/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/rand/seq/index.html)

`seq`use rand::prelude::*; if rand::random() { // generates a boolean // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)! println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>()); } let mut rng = rand::thread_rng(); let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1 let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect(); nums.shuffle(&mut rng);

# wasm_timer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-timer/^0.2/

[Skip to main content](#main-content)# Crate wasm_timer

[Source](../src/wasm_timer/lib.rs.html#21-30) - [ext](ext/index.html)
- Extension traits for the standard `Stream`and`Future`traits.

- [Delay](struct.Delay.html)
- A future representing the notification that an elapsed duration has
occurred.
- [Instant](struct.Instant.html)
- A measurement of a monotonically nondecreasing clock.
Opaque and useful only with `Duration`
- [Interval](struct.Interval.html)
- A stream representing notifications at fixed interval
- [SetDefaultError](struct.SetDefaultError.html)
- Error returned from `TimerHandle::set_fallback`.
- [SystemTime](struct.SystemTime.html)
- A measurement of the system clock, useful for talking to
external entities like the file system or other processes.
- [Timer](struct.Timer.html)
- A “timer heap” used to power separately owned instances of `Delay`and`Interval`.
- [TimerHandle](struct.TimerHandle.html)
- A handle to a `Timer`which is used to create instances of a`Delay`.

- [UNIX_EPOCH](constant.UNIX_EPOCH.html)
- An anchor in time which can be used to create new `SystemTime`instances or
learn about where in time a`SystemTime`lies.

- [TryFutureExt](trait.TryFutureExt.html)
- An extension trait for futures which provides convenient accessors for
timing out execution and such.
- [TryStreamExt](trait.TryStreamExt.html)
- An extension trait for streams which provides convenient accessors for
timing out execution and such.

# pretty_env_logger - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pretty_env_logger/^0.4/

A logger configured via an environment variable which writes to standard error with nice colored output for log levels.

extern crate pretty_env_logger; #[macro_use] extern crate log; fn main() { pretty_env_logger::init(); trace!("a trace example"); debug!("deboogging"); info!("such information"); warn!("o_O"); error!("boom"); }

Run the program with the environment variable `RUST_LOG=trace`.

The defaults can be setup by calling `init()` or `try_init()` at the start
of the program.

This crate uses [env_logger](https://docs.rs/env_logger) internally, so the same ways of enabling
logs through an environment variable are supported.

# reqwest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reqwest/^0.10/

The `reqwest` crate provides a convenient, higher-level HTTP
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html).

It handles many of the things that most people just expect an HTTP client to do for them.

- Async and [blocking](https://docs.rs/reqwest/blocking/index.html)Clients
- Plain bodies, [JSON](https://docs.rs#json),[urlencoded](https://docs.rs#forms),[multipart](https://docs.rs/reqwest/multipart/index.html)
- Customizable [redirect policy](https://docs.rs#redirect-policies)
- HTTP [Proxies](https://docs.rs#proxies)
- Uses system-native [TLS](https://docs.rs#tls)
- Cookies

The [ reqwest::Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) is asynchronous. For applications wishing
to only make a few HTTP requests, the

[API may be more convenient.](https://docs.rs/reqwest/blocking/index.html)

`reqwest::blocking`Additional learning resources include:

For a single request, you can use the [ get](https://docs.rs/fn.get.html) shortcut method.

let body = reqwest::get("https://www.rust-lang.org") .await? .text() .await?; println!("body = {:?}", body);

**NOTE**: If you plan to perform multiple requests, it is best to create a
[ Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) and reuse it, taking advantage of keep-alive connection
pooling.

There are several ways you can set the body of a request. The basic one is
by using the `body()` method of a [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html). This lets you set the
exact raw bytes of what the body should be. It accepts various types,
including

`String`, `Vec<u8>`, and `File`. If you wish to pass a custom
type, you can use the `reqwest::Body` constructors.let client = reqwest::Client::new(); let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post") .body("the exact body that is sent") .send() .await?;

It's very common to want to send form data in a request body. This can be done with any type that can be serialized into form data.

This can be an array of tuples, or a `HashMap`, or a custom type that
implements [ Serialize](http://serde.rs).

// This will POST a body of `foo=bar&baz=quux` let params = [("foo", "bar"), ("baz", "quux")]; let client = reqwest::Client::new(); let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post") .form(¶ms) .send() .await?;

There is also a `json` method helper on the [ RequestBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBuilder.html) that works in
a similar fashion the

`form` method. It can take any value that can be
serialized into JSON. The feature `json` is required.// This will POST a body of `{"lang":"rust","body":"json"}` let mut map = HashMap::new(); map.insert("lang", "rust"); map.insert("body", "json"); let client = reqwest::Client::new(); let res = client.post("http://httpbin.org/post") .json(&map) .send() .await?;

By default, a `Client` will automatically handle HTTP redirects, having a
maximum redirect chain of 10 hops. To customize this behavior, a
[ redirect::Policy](https://docs.rs/reqwest/redirect/index.html) can be used with a

`ClientBuilder`.The automatic storing and sending of session cookies can be enabled with
the [ cookie_store](https://docs.rs/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.cookie_store) method on

`ClientBuilder`.**NOTE**: System proxies are enabled by default.

System proxies look in environment variables to set HTTP or HTTPS proxies.

`HTTP_PROXY` or `http_proxy` provide http proxies for http connections while
`HTTPS_PROXY` or `https_proxy` provide HTTPS proxies for HTTPS connections.

These can be overwritten by adding a [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/reqwest/struct.Proxy.html) to

`ClientBuilder`
i.e. `let proxy = reqwest::Proxy::http("https://secure.example")?;`
or disabled by calling `ClientBuilder::no_proxy()`.`socks` feature is required if you have configured socks proxy like this:

```
export https_proxy=socks5://127.0.0.1:1086
```
By default, a `Client` will make use of system-native transport layer
security to connect to HTTPS destinations. This means schannel on Windows,
Security-Framework on macOS, and OpenSSL on Linux.

- Additional X509 certificates can be configured on a `ClientBuilder`with the`Certificate`
- Client certificates can be add to a `ClientBuilder`with the`Identity`
- Various parts of TLS can also be configured or even disabled on the
`ClientBuilder`.

The following are a list of [Cargo features](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) that can be
enabled or disabled:

- **default-tls**- *(enabled by default)*: Provides TLS support to connect over HTTPS.
- **native-tls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `native-tls`.
- **native-tls-vendored**: Enables the- `vendored`feature of- `native-tls`.
- **rustls-tls**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`. Equivalent to- `rustls-tls-webpki-roots`.
- **rustls-tls-manual-roots**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`, without setting any root certificates. Roots have to be specified manually.
- **rustls-tls-webpki-roots**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`, while using root certificates from the- `webpki-roots`crate.
- **rustls-tls-native-roots**: Enables TLS functionality provided by- `rustls`, while using root certificates from the- `rustls-native-certs`crate.
- **blocking**: Provides the- [blocking](https://docs.rs/blocking/index.html)client API.
- **cookies**: Provides cookie session support.
- **gzip**: Provides response body gzip decompression.
- **brotli**: Provides response body brotli decompression.
- **json**: Provides serialization and deserialization for JSON bodies.
- **stream**: Adds support for- `futures::Stream`.
- **socks**: Provides SOCKS5 proxy support.
- **trust-dns**: Enables a trust-dns async resolver instead of default threadpool using- `getaddrinfo`.

# tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokio/^0.2/

A runtime for writing reliable, asynchronous, and slim applications.

Tokio is an event-driven, non-blocking I/O platform for writing asynchronous applications with the Rust programming language. At a high level, it provides a few major components:

- Tools for [working with asynchronous tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks), including[synchronization primitives and channels](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/index.html)and[timeouts, delays, and intervals](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/index.html).
- APIs for [performing asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io), including[TCP and UDP](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/index.html)sockets,[filesystem](https://docs.rs/tokio/fs/index.html)operations, and[process](https://docs.rs/tokio/process/index.html)and[signal](https://docs.rs/tokio/signal/index.html)management.
- A [runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/index.html)for executing asynchronous code, including a task scheduler, an I/O driver backed by the operating system's event queue (epoll, kqueue, IOCP, etc...), and a high performance timer.

Guide level documentation is found on the [website](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial).

Tokio consists of a number of modules that provide a range of functionality essential for implementing asynchronous applications in Rust. In this section, we will take a brief tour of Tokio, summarizing the major APIs and their uses.

The easiest way to get started is to enable all features. Do this by
enabling the `full` feature flag:

```
tokio = { version = "0.2", features = ["full"] }
```
Tokio uses a set of [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) to reduce the amount of compiled code. It
is possible to just enable certain features over others. By default, Tokio
does not enable any features but allows one to enable a subset for their use
case. Below is a list of the available feature flags. You may also notice
above each function, struct and trait there is listed one or more feature flags
that are required for that item to be used. If you are new to Tokio it is
recommended that you use the `full` feature flag which will enable all public APIs.
Beware though that this will pull in many extra dependencies that you may not
need.

- `full`: Enables all Tokio public API features listed below.
- `rt-core`: Enables- `tokio::spawn`and the basic (single-threaded) scheduler.
- `rt-threaded`: Enables the heavier, multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler.
- `rt-util`: Enables non-scheduler utilities.
- `io-driver`: Enables the- `mio`based IO driver.
- `io-util`: Enables the IO based- `Ext`traits.
- `io-std`: Enable- `Stdout`,- `Stdin`and- `Stderr`types.
- `net`: Enables- `tokio::net`types such as- `TcpStream`,- `UnixStream`and- `UdpSocket`.
- `tcp`: Enables all- `tokio::net::tcp`types.
- `udp`: Enables all- `tokio::net::udp`types.
- `uds`: Enables all- `tokio::net::unix`types.
- `time`: Enables- `tokio::time`types and allows the schedulers to enable the built in timer.
- `process`: Enables- `tokio::process`types.
- `macros`: Enables- `#[tokio::main]`and- `#[tokio::test]`macros.
- `sync`: Enables all- `tokio::sync`types.
- `stream`: Enables optional- `Stream`implementations for types within Tokio.
- `signal`: Enables all- `tokio::signal`types.
- `fs`: Enables- `tokio::fs`types.
- `dns`: Enables async- `tokio::net::ToSocketAddrs`.
- `test-util`: Enables testing based infrastructure for the Tokio runtime.
- `blocking`: Enables- `block_in_place`and- `spawn_blocking`.

*Note:  AsyncRead and AsyncWrite traits do not require any features and are
always available.*

These features do not expose any new API, but influence internal
implementation aspects of Tokio, and can pull in additional
dependencies. They are not included in `full`:

- `parking_lot`: As a potential optimization, use the- *parking_lot*crate's synchronization primitives internally. MSRV may increase according to the- *parking_lot*release in use.

Tokio is great for writing applications and most users in this case shouldn't
worry too much about what features they should pick. If you're unsure, we suggest
going with `full` to ensure that you don't run into any road blocks while you're
building your application.

This example shows the quickest way to get started with Tokio.

```
tokio = { version = "0.2", features = ["full"] }
```
As a library author your goal should be to provide the lighest weight crate that is based on Tokio. To achieve this you should ensure that you only enable the features you need. This allows users to pick up your crate without having to enable unnecessary features.

This example shows how you may want to import features for a library that just
needs to `tokio::spawn` and use a `TcpStream`.

```
tokio = { version = "0.2", features = ["rt-core", "tcp"] }
```
Asynchronous programs in Rust are based around lightweight, non-blocking
units of execution called [ tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks). The

[module provides important tools for working with tasks:](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/index.html)

`tokio::task`- The `spawn``JoinHandle`
- Functions for [running blocking operations](https://docs.rs/task/index.html#blocking-and-yielding)in an asynchronous task context.

The [ tokio::task](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/index.html) module is present only when the "rt-core" feature flag
is enabled.

The [ tokio::sync](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/index.html) module contains synchronization primitives to use when
needing to communicate or share data. These include:

- channels (`oneshot``mpsc``watch`
- a non-blocking `Mutex`
- an asynchronous `Barrier`

The `tokio::sync` module is present only when the "sync" feature flag is
enabled.

The [ tokio::time](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/index.html) module provides utilities for tracking time and
scheduling work. This includes functions for setting

[timeouts](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/fn.timeout.html)for tasks,

[delaying](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/fn.delay_for.html)work to run in the future, or

[repeating an operation at an interval](https://docs.rs/tokio/time/fn.interval.html).

In order to use `tokio::time`, the "time" feature flag must be enabled.

Finally, Tokio provides a *runtime* for executing asynchronous tasks. Most
applications can use the [ #[tokio::main]](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html) macro to run their code on the
Tokio runtime. In use-cases where manual control over the runtime is
required, the

[module provides APIs for configuring and managing runtimes.](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/index.html)

`tokio::runtime`Using the runtime requires the "rt-core" or "rt-threaded" feature flags, to
enable the basic [single-threaded scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#basic-scheduler) and the [thread-pool
scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#threaded-scheduler), respectively. See the [ runtime module
documentation](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#runtime-scheduler) for details. In addition, the "macros" feature
flag enables the

`#[tokio::main]` and `#[tokio::test]` attributes.Tokio is able to concurrently run many tasks on a few threads by repeatedly
swapping the currently running task on each thread. However, this kind of
swapping can only happen at `.await` points, so code that spends a long time
without reaching an `.await` will prevent other tasks from running. To
combat this, Tokio provides two kinds of threads: Core threads and blocking
threads. The core threads are where all asynchronous code runs, and Tokio
will by default spawn one for each CPU core. The blocking threads are
spawned on demand, and can be used to run blocking code that would otherwise
block other tasks from running. Since it is not possible for Tokio to swap
out blocking tasks, like it can do with asynchronous code, the upper limit
on the number of blocking threads is very large. These limits can be
configured on the [ Builder](https://docs.rs/tokio/runtime/struct.Builder.html).

To spawn a blocking task, you should use the [ spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/tokio/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html) function.

#[tokio::main] async fn main() { // This is running on a core thread. let blocking_task = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| { // This is running on a blocking thread. // Blocking here is ok. }); // We can wait for the blocking task like this: // If the blocking task panics, the unwrap below will propagate the // panic. blocking_task.await.unwrap(); }

If your code is CPU-bound and you wish to limit the number of threads used
to run it, you should run it on another thread pool such as [rayon](https://docs.rs/rayon). You
can use an [ oneshot](https://docs.rs/tokio/sync/oneshot/index.html) channel to send the result back to Tokio when the
rayon task finishes.

As well as scheduling and running tasks, Tokio provides everything you need to perform input and output asynchronously.

The [ tokio::io](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/index.html) module provides Tokio's asynchronous core I/O primitives,
the

[,](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/trait.AsyncRead.html)

`AsyncRead`[, and](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/trait.AsyncWrite.html)

`AsyncWrite`[traits. In addition, when the "io-util" feature flag is enabled, it also provides combinators and functions for working with these traits, forming as an asynchronous counterpart to](https://docs.rs/tokio/io/trait.AsyncBufRead.html)

`AsyncBufRead`[. When the "io-driver" feature flag is enabled, it also provides utilities for library authors implementing I/O resources.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/index.html)

`std::io`Tokio also includes APIs for performing various kinds of I/O and interacting with the operating system asynchronously. These include:

- `tokio::net`- [TCP](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/tcp/index.html),- [UDP](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/udp/index.html), and- [Unix Domain Sockets](https://docs.rs/tokio/net/unix/index.html)(enabled by the "net" feature flag),
- `tokio::fs`- `std::fs`
- `tokio::signal`
- `tokio::process`

A simple TCP echo server:

use tokio::net::TcpListener; use tokio::prelude::*; #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let mut listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?; loop { let (mut socket, _) = listener.accept().await?; tokio::spawn(async move { let mut buf = [0; 1024]; // In a loop, read data from the socket and write the data back. loop { let n = match socket.read(&mut buf).await { // socket closed Ok(n) if n == 0 => return, Ok(n) => n, Err(e) => { eprintln!("failed to read from socket; err = {:?}", e); return; } }; // Write the data back if let Err(e) = socket.write_all(&buf[0..n]).await { eprintln!("failed to write to socket; err = {:?}", e); return; } } }); } }

| [fs](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html) | `fs`Asynchronous file and standard stream adaptation. |
| [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) | Traits, helpers, and type definitions for asynchronous I/O functionality. |
| [net](https://docs.rs/net/index.html) | TCP/UDP/Unix bindings for  |

# again - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/again/latest/target-redirect/again/

## Expand description

`Again` is a wasm-compatible utility for retrying standard library [ Futures](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/future/trait.Future.html) with a

`Result` output typeA goal of any operation should be a successful outcome. This crate gives operations a better chance at achieving that.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#hello-world)Hello world

For simple cases, you can use the module level [ retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html) fn, which
will retry a task every second for 5 seconds with an exponential backoff.

`again::retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));`[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-retries)Conditional retries

By default, `again` will retry any failed `Future` if its `Result` output type is an `Err`.
You may not want to retry *every* kind of error. In those cases you may wish to use the [ retry_if](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_if.html) fn, which
accepts an additional argument to conditionally determine if the error
should be retried.

```
again::retry_if(
    || reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"),
    reqwest::Error::is_status,
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#retry-policies)Retry policies

Every application has different needs. The default retry behavior in `again`
likely will not suit all of them. You can define your own retry behavior
with a [ RetryPolicy](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html). A RetryPolicy can be configured with a fixed or exponential backoff,
jitter, and other common retry options. This objects may be reused
across operations. For more information see the

[docs.](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)

`RetryPolicy`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use again::RetryPolicy;
use std::time::Duration;
let policy = RetryPolicy::fixed(Duration::from_millis(100))
    .with_max_retries(10)
    .with_jitter(false);
policy.retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

For visibility on when operations fail and are retried, a `log::trace` message is emitted,
logging the `Debug` display of the error and the delay before the next attempt.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-features)wasm features

`again` supports [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/) targets i.e. `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which should make this
crate a good fit for most environments

Two cargo features exist to support various wasm runtimes: `wasm-bindgen` and `stdweb`.
To enable them add the following to your `Cargo.toml` file.

```
[dependencies]
again = { version = "xxx", features = ["wasm-bindgen"] }
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Retry](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)- Policy
- A template for configuring retry behavior

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# facett_icebergview - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-icebergview/0.1.10/facett_icebergview/

## Expand description

**facett-icebergview** — browse **and time-travel** one Iceberg table, drawn
from **Arrow  RecordBatches**. The component is

*engine-agnostic*: you hand it, per Iceberg snapshot, the snapshot’s metadata + its materialized Arrow frame; it renders a

**snapshot picker**(newest-first, showing snapshot id / timestamp / row-count) over a virtualized,

**paged**row grid (the rows come from

[, built from the batch via](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[). Selecting a snapshot loads](https://docs.rs/facett-arrow/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_arrow/index.html)

`facett_arrow`*that*snapshot’s frame — time travel.

Like every facett component it implements [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html) (

`title` / `ui` /
`state_json`), so it drops into a `FacetDeck` and is robot-testable through
`facett_core::harness`: drive [/](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.select_snapshot)

`IcebergView::select_snapshot`[headlessly and assert](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.set_page)

`IcebergView::set_page``state_json` (the current snapshot, the snapshot list,
and the visible rows all change). `state_json` exposes:- `table`— the table name,
- `snapshots`— every snapshot newest-first (- `id`,- `timestamp_ms`,- `rows`),
- `current`— the selected snapshot id,
- `total_rows`/- `page`/- `page_size`/- `visible_rows`— the paged view.

**Why not just  facett-table?** A table viewer shows

*one*frame. This adds the Iceberg dimension — the history of snapshots and the control to scrub between them — which is the whole point of a lakehouse table browser. The adapter that

*fills*it from a real catalog (skade) lives host-side (korp / nornir) so this crate never takes a hard catalog/engine dependency.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iceberg](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html)- View
- A browse + time-travel viewer for one Iceberg table.
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.Snapshot.html)
- One snapshot paired with the Arrow frame that materializes it. The frame is a
`Vec<RecordBatch>`exactly as a scan returns it;`IcebergView`concatenates the rows into a paged`Table`
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.SnapshotMeta.html)- Meta
- One Iceberg snapshot’s identity, for the picker + `state_json`. Mirrors what`iceberg::spec::Snapshot`exposes (`snapshot_id()`/`timestamp_ms()`) plus a row count the host computes (scan count, or the snapshot summary’s`total-records`).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE.html)- PAGE_ - SIZE
- Default rows shown per page (the Table is virtualized, but paging keeps a huge
snapshot from being cell-formatted all at once and makes `visible_rows`meaningful for headless assertions).

# facett_warehousedeck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-warehousedeck/0.1.10/facett_warehousedeck/

## Expand description

**facett-warehousedeck** — a multi-pane **dashboard over a lakehouse
warehouse**. It views the warehouse as **many components at once**: several
**3D graphs** (call graph, dependency graph, world-delta, release lineage,
SBOM/vuln) **plus** grids and charts, all visible simultaneously in a wall.

It is built **entirely from existing facett widgets** — it never reimplements
a viewer. Each pane is one of:
[ facett_graph3d::Graph3D](https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph3d/struct.Graph3D.html) ·

[/](https://docs.rs/facett-grid/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_grid/struct.Grid.html)

`facett_grid::Grid`[·](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[, composed inside a](https://docs.rs/facett-plot/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_plot/struct.PlotView.html)

`facett_plot::PlotView`[. The deck is rendered in](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html)

`facett_core::FacetDeck`**Wall**mode (

[) so every pane (and thus several](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.wall_ui)

`FacetDeck::wall_ui``Graph3D` instances) draws at once; a **Focus**mode falls back to the deck’s tabbed

[.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.ui)

`FacetDeck::ui`[§](https://docs.rs#engine-agnostic)Engine-agnostic

Like the rest of facett, this crate takes **data, not a catalog**: a host
(nornir’s viz) opens its Iceberg warehouse, reads each table, maps the rows to
a [ PaneData](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html) view-model, and hands them in. This crate never depends on
iceberg/skade/nornir.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-registry-table--view-kind)The registry (table → view-kind)

[ WarehouseRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseRegistry.html) maps a

**table name**to the

[it should render as, so adding a table is one](https://docs.rs/enum.ViewKind.html)

`ViewKind``register(...)` line. The host queries the
registry to decide which [to build for a table; explicit join-panes (e.g. the call graph from](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html)

`PaneData``call_edges`×`symbol_facts`) are added directly.[§](https://docs.rs#robot-testable)Robot-testable

[ WarehouseDeck](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html) is itself a

[, so it drops into nornir’s viz and is headless-assertable.](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet`[exposes](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html#method.state_json)

`WarehouseDeck::state_json``pane_count`,
per-kind counts (`graph3d_count`, `grid_count`, …), and a `panes` array
carrying each pane’s `nodes`/`edges`/`rows`/`series`, plus the composed deck
state (whose `trace.ran` lists `deck.wall:<title>` for every pane that drew).## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chart](https://docs.rs/struct.ChartSpec.html)- Spec
- A chart view-model: named `(x, y)`series + the chart kind. Maps onto`PlotView`
- [Color32](https://docs.rs/struct.Color32.html)
- This format is used for space-efficient color representation (32 bits).
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphSpec.html)- Spec
- A 3D-graph view-model: `(label, color)`nodes + index edges + a layout. Maps directly onto`Graph3D::new`
- [Pane](https://docs.rs/struct.PaneInfo.html)- Info
- Per-pane metadata, mirrored into `state_json`for headless assertions.
- [Warehouse](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html)- Deck

# sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer-riemann/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann/

## Expand description

Neo-Riemannian / functional triad naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate implements the Riemannian naming school: it labels a triad by its
functional quality relative to its root, distinguishing a major triad (`T`,
upper-case for the major tonic function) from a minor triad (`t`,
lower-case). [ label_riemann](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html) rotates the pitch-class set so the root sits at
zero and matches the major or minor triad signature; non-triadic sets return

`None`.## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [label_](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html)- riemann
- Labels `mask`as a major (`T`) or minor (`t`) triad relative to its root.

# facett_security - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-security/0.1.10/facett_security/

## Expand description

**facett-security** — a software-supply-chain **security report** view: the
**verdict** (Pass / Warn / Block), the **findings** list (id · severity ·
package · advisory · fix) with **severity / EPSS / KEV** columns, and a
secondary **CVE / advisory** reference table. It is the UI *twin* of
[modgunn](https://codeberg.org/nordisk/modgunn)’s scan output — the gate that
decides whether an artifact may be served / promoted.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-on-purpose-no-modgunn-dependency)Generic on purpose (no modgunn dependency)

facett MUST NOT couple to the modgunn crate. So this crate carries its **own**
plain, serializable structs — [ Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)

`Severity`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)

`Finding`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`[— whose shape](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)

`SecurityReport`**mirrors**so a consumer (nornir-viz / holger-ui) maps the two

`modgunn::core`**1:1**with no glue:

| facett-security | modgunn::core |
|---|---|
| (Pass/Warn/Block)`Verdict` | `Decision`(Pass/Warn/Block) — same`Ord` |
| (Info…Critical)`Severity` | `Severity`(Info…Critical) — same`Ord` |
| `Finding``{id,severity,…}` | `Finding``{id,severity,summary}`(superset) |
| `Artifact` | `ArtifactRef` |
| `SecurityReport` | `Verdict`(the whole cacheable result) |

[ Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html) is a

**superset**: modgunn’s three fields map straight in, and the richer scan columns the UI wants (

`package`, `advisory`, `fix`, `epss`, `kev`)
are optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has and leaves the rest defaulted.[§](https://docs.rs#fc-compliance-the-component-contract)FC compliance (the component contract)

- **FC-1 / FC-3**— all observable state lives in one serializable- `SecurityState`- `Serialize`/- `Deserialize`/- `Clone`/- `PartialEq`), read back via- `SecurityView::state`
- **FC-2 / FC-9**— every input is a- `Msg`- `SecurityView::update`- `render`- `&self`that paints and- *returns*the- `Msg`- `Facet::ui`
- **FC-4**— the painted verdict pill emits an AccessKit node; every finding row / CVE row is a selectable, labelled, value-carrying node.
- **FC-5**— rows are keyed off the finding- **id**(a stable domain key), never a loop index.
- **FC-6**— pure egui + painter, renders headlessly (the deck robot path).
- **FC-7**— no ambient clock / RNG / animation: the scan time is an- *injected*host-stamped string (- `SecurityReport::scanned_at`
- **FC-8**— the view does no I/O;- `SecurityView::is_idle`- `SecurityView::update`- `Vec<Effect>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- The artifact a verdict is about (content-addressed). Mirrors
`modgunn::core::ArtifactRef`.
- [Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)
- One thing the scanner found. `id`,`severity`,`summary`map straight from`modgunn::core::Finding`; the rest are the richer scan columns the UI shows (all optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has).
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)- Report
- The cacheable scan result: the verdict + its findings + the keys it was
computed against. The plain data a host hands the view; mirrors the whole of
`modgunn::core::Verdict`.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityState.html)- State
- **All**observable state for the view (FC-1 / FC-3): the report plus the UI state (the drilled-in finding, the severity floor filter, and the zoom). Fully serializable so a caller reads it back at any frame boundary.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityView.html)- View
- The `Facet``SecurityReport`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Effect](https://docs.rs/enum.Effect.html)
- Side work as data (FC-8). The view does no I/O, so this is uninhabited — it exists to make the “no pending effects” contract explicit and type-checked.
- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- Every input the view accepts (FC-2). The **only**legal way to mutate`SecurityState``Debug`+`Clone`.
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Finding severity (declaration order = ascending, so the worst finding is the
`max()`). Mirrors`modgunn::core::Severity`.
- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html)
- What a gate should DO with the artifact, given the findings. Declaration
order is the strictness order — `Pass < Warn < Block`— so folding many findings into one verdict is their`Ord::max``modgunn::core::Decision`relies on).

# facett_plandag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-plandag/0.1.10/facett_plandag/

## Expand description

**facett-plandag** — a **metric-bearing operator DAG**: the Spark **SQL query
plan** / Databricks **Query Profile graph**. Each node carries a multi-line
**metric body** (time / memory / rows / spill); a **cost-heat** switch
(Time / Memory / Rows) fills nodes by relative cost; **WholeStageCodegen groups**
collapse into super-nodes; and an **AQE initial-vs-final** toggle flips between
the two plan versions. The four things the doc says no single facett graph had
at once.

It **composes** facett’s existing graph stack — exactly the documented “compose
`facett_graph`, paint our own” pattern:

- `facett_graph::DepGraphView`- **column layering**+- `facett_graph::draw_arrow`
- [`facett_pipeline::Status`] supplies the**themed node-status colour**.
- The pure, serializable `model`

[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`): the resolved graph (every node’s metric body + its- **cost-heat as DATA**), the active metric/version, the collapse set, the selection.
- `Msg`- `PlanDagView::update`
- **Render-proof**: the painter and- `state_json`both read from one- `model::resolve`

# facett_helix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-helix/0.1.10/facett_helix/

## Expand description

**facett-helix** — the **TIME-HELIX DAG view**. A plan / dependency DAG rendered
as a **helix that advances ALONG a time axis**: each node is a plan item (idea /
task / test / crate) tied to a `system` (its angular lane / strand); the DAG winds
*forward through time* rather than spinning in place. Edges are **soft rounded
rubberband splines** (Catmull-Rom, elastic settle); coils can be **wound onto a
pin** (`wind`); many coils coexist in one scene with **inter-helix links**; an
**animated traverse** flies a time-cursor along the axis. GPU-rendered with the
emissive **bloom** lane reused from `facett-graph3d`.

[§](https://docs.rs#portability-contract-the-reason-this-crate-exists)Portability contract (the reason this crate exists)

[ model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html) +

[depend on](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)

`layout`**nothing but**— no egui, no facett, no nornir/modgunn. They are the seam that

`serde` + `std``git mv`s into **ordning**. Only

[(this file) binds to facett’s](https://docs.rs/struct.HelixView.html)

`HelixView`[/egui/](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet``facett-graph3d`. Hosts
(nornir’s funnel, modgunn) just *populate*a

[through the](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Scene.html)

`model::Scene`[API; facett stays generic.](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanDag.html#method.add_idea)

`model::PlanDag::add_idea`[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`- `t`, angular lane, system) + the wind / level / cursor / tension — the picture asserted as DATA.
- `Msg`- `update`
- **Injected clock**(- `set_clock`- `Msg::Tick`
- **AccessKit**: each node rides into the tree as a queryable Button (FC-4).

# everruns_a2ui - Rust

## Expand description

A2UI component catalog and prompt generator for Everruns.

Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to emit A2UI JSON component trees. The JSON is transported in ```a2ui fenced code blocks and rendered by the UI using native shadcn/ui primitives.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_a2ui::{PromptOptions, default_catalog, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_catalog(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```a2ui"));
```

# everruns_openui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-openui/0.17.3/everruns_openui/

## Expand description

OpenUI component library and prompt generator for Everruns.

Rust reimplementation of the OpenUI component definitions and prompt generator. Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to generate OpenUI Lang code.

The generated prompt is compatible with `@openuidev/react-lang` and `@openuidev/react-ui`
— the React runtime parses the LLM output and renders it into interactive components.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_openui::{PromptOptions, default_library, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_library(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```openui"));
```
Ref: [https://github.com/thesysdev/openui](https://github.com/thesysdev/openui)

- Component definitions: packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib/
- Prompt generator: packages/react-lang/src/parser/prompt.ts
- Library/types: packages/react-lang/src/library.ts

# athena_pipelines - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/athena-pipelines/3.26.3/athena_pipelines/

## Expand description

Portable Athena pipeline contracts and request-domain helpers.

This crate owns the declarative pipeline model that can be shared across the
server runtime, admin APIs, CLI/bootstrap loading, and future adapters
without depending on Actix or `AppState`.

The current scope covers:

- source/transform/sink pipeline DTOs,
- pipeline request payloads and template summaries,
- persisted template DTOs and record-to-runtime conversion helpers,
- pipeline template SQL adapters and step-log persistence helpers,
- request-independent pipeline execution orchestration behind runtime traits,
- database-backed template catalog loaders and list response contracts,
- YAML registry loading for named pipelines,
- validation and template/override resolution,
- template-name normalization and boot-template shadow policy helpers,
- gateway fetch-body construction and row alias rewriting.
- pipeline execution response contracts shared by runtime handlers and tests.

# again 0.1.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/again/0.1.2

A goal of any operation should be a successful outcome. This crate gives operations a better chance at achieving that.

## 📦 install

In your Cargo.toml file, add the following under the `[dependencies]` heading

```
 = "0.1"
```
## 🤸usage

For very simple cases you can use the module level `retry` function
to retry a potentially fallible operation.

```
use Error;
async
```
You may not want to retry *every* kind of error. For preciseness you can be more explicit in which kinds of errors should be retried with the module level `retry_if` function.

```
use Error;
async
```
You can also customize retry behavior to suit your applications needs
with a configurable and reusable `RetryPolicy`.

```
use Error;
use Duration;
use RetryPolicy;
async
```
See the [docs](http://docs.rs/again) for more examples.

Doug Tangren (softprops) 2020

# again - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/again/0.1.2/target-redirect/again/

## Expand description

`Again` is a wasm-compatible utility for retrying standard library [ Futures](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/future/trait.Future.html) with a

`Result` output typeA goal of any operation should be a successful outcome. This crate gives operations a better chance at achieving that.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#hello-world)Hello world

For simple cases, you can use the module level [ retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html) fn, which
will retry a task every second for 5 seconds with an exponential backoff.

`again::retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));`[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-retries)Conditional retries

By default, `again` will retry any failed `Future` if its `Result` output type is an `Err`.
You may not want to retry *every* kind of error. In those cases you may wish to use the [ retry_if](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_if.html) fn, which
accepts an additional argument to conditionally determine if the error
should be retried.

```
again::retry_if(
    || reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"),
    reqwest::Error::is_status,
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#retry-policies)Retry policies

Every application has different needs. The default retry behavior in `again`
likely will not suit all of them. You can define your own retry behavior
with a [ RetryPolicy](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html). A RetryPolicy can be configured with a fixed or exponential backoff,
jitter, and other common retry options. This objects may be reused
across operations. For more information see the

[docs.](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)

`RetryPolicy`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use again::RetryPolicy;
use std::time::Duration;
let policy = RetryPolicy::fixed(Duration::from_millis(100))
    .with_max_retries(10)
    .with_jitter(false);
policy.retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

For visibility on when operations fail and are retried, a `log::trace` message is emitted,
logging the `Debug` display of the error and the delay before the next attempt.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-features)wasm features

`again` supports [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/) targets i.e. `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which should make this
crate a good fit for most environments

Two cargo features exist to support various wasm runtimes: `wasm-bindgen` and `stdweb`.
To enable them add the following to your `Cargo.toml` file.

```
[dependencies]
again = { version = "xxx", features = ["wasm-bindgen"] }
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Retry](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)- Policy
- A template for configuring retry behavior

[132](https://docs.rs#132)    jitter: bool,
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    delay: Duration,
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    max_delay: Option<Duration>,
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    max_retries: usize,
[136](https://docs.rs#136)}
[137](https://docs.rs#137)
[138](https://docs.rs#138)impl Iterator for BackoffIter {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    type Item = Duration;
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
[141](https://docs.rs#141)        if self.max_retries > 0 {
[142](https://docs.rs#142)            let factor = match self.backoff {
[143](https://docs.rs#143)                Backoff::Fixed => Some(self.current),
[144](https://docs.rs#144)                Backoff::Exponential => {
[145](https://docs.rs#145)                    let factor = self.current;
[146](https://docs.rs#146)                    if let Some(next) = self.current.checked_mul(2) {
[147](https://docs.rs#147)                        self.current = next;
[148](https://docs.rs#148)                    } else {
[149](https://docs.rs#149)                        self.current = u32::MAX;
[150](https://docs.rs#150)                    }
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)                    Some(factor)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)                }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)            };
[155](https://docs.rs#155)
[156](https://docs.rs#156)            if let Some(factor) = factor {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)                if let Some(mut delay) = self.delay.checked_mul(factor) {
[158](https://docs.rs#158)                    #[cfg(feature = "rand")]
[159](https://docs.rs#159)                    {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)                        if self.jitter {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)                            delay = jitter(delay);
[162](https://docs.rs#162)                        }
[163](https://docs.rs#163)                    }
[164](https://docs.rs#164)                    if let Some(max_delay) = self.max_delay {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)                        delay = min(delay, max_delay);
[166](https://docs.rs#166)                    }
[167](https://docs.rs#167)                    self.max_retries -= 1;
[168](https://docs.rs#168)                    return Some(delay);
[169](https://docs.rs#169)                }
[170](https://docs.rs#170)            }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)        }
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        None
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    }
[174](https://docs.rs#174)}

[204](https://docs.rs#204)#[cfg(feature = "rand")]
[205](https://docs.rs#205)fn jitter(duration: Duration) -> Duration {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    let jitter: f64 = thread_rng().sample(OpenClosed01);
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    let secs = (duration.as_secs() as f64) * jitter;
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    let nanos = (duration.subsec_nanos() as f64) * jitter;
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    let millis = (secs * 1_000_f64) + (nanos / 1_000_000_f64);
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    Duration::from_millis(millis as u64)
[211](https://docs.rs#211)}

[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// Retries a fallible `Future` with this policy's configuration under certain provided conditions
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    pub async fn retry_if<T, C>(
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        &self,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        task: T,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        condition: C,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    ) -> Result<T::Item, T::Error>
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    where
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        T: Task,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        C: Condition<T::Error>,
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        let mut backoffs = self.backoffs();
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        let mut task = task;
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        let mut condition = condition;
[305](https://docs.rs#305)        loop {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)            match task.call().await {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)                Ok(result) => return Ok(result),
[308](https://docs.rs#308)                Err(err) => {
[309](https://docs.rs#309)                    if condition.is_retryable(&err) {
[310](https://docs.rs#310)                        if let Some(delay) = backoffs.next() {
[311](https://docs.rs#311)                            #[cfg(feature = "log")]
[312](https://docs.rs#312)                            {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)                                log::trace!(
[314](https://docs.rs#314)                                    "task failed with error {:?}. will try again in {:?}",
[315](https://docs.rs#315)                                    err,
[316](https://docs.rs#316)                                    delay
[317](https://docs.rs#317)                                );
[318](https://docs.rs#318)                            }
[319](https://docs.rs#319)                            let _ = Delay::new(delay).await;
[320](https://docs.rs#320)                            continue;
[321](https://docs.rs#321)                        }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)                    }
[323](https://docs.rs#323)                    return Err(err);
[324](https://docs.rs#324)                }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            }
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        }
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    }

# again - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/again/latest/again/

## Expand description

`Again` is a wasm-compatible utility for retrying standard library [ Futures](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/future/trait.Future.html) with a

`Result` output typeA goal of any operation should be a successful outcome. This crate gives operations a better chance at achieving that.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#hello-world)Hello world

For simple cases, you can use the module level [ retry](https://docs.rs/fn.retry.html) fn, which
will retry a task every second for 5 seconds with an exponential backoff.

`again::retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));`[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-retries)Conditional retries

By default, `again` will retry any failed `Future` if its `Result` output type is an `Err`.
You may not want to retry *every* kind of error. In those cases you may wish to use the [ retry_if](https://docs.rs/fn.retry_if.html) fn, which
accepts an additional argument to conditionally determine if the error
should be retried.

```
again::retry_if(
    || reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"),
    reqwest::Error::is_status,
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#retry-policies)Retry policies

Every application has different needs. The default retry behavior in `again`
likely will not suit all of them. You can define your own retry behavior
with a [ RetryPolicy](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html). A RetryPolicy can be configured with a fixed or exponential backoff,
jitter, and other common retry options. This objects may be reused
across operations. For more information see the

[docs.](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)

`RetryPolicy`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use again::RetryPolicy;
use std::time::Duration;
let policy = RetryPolicy::fixed(Duration::from_millis(100))
    .with_max_retries(10)
    .with_jitter(false);
policy.retry(|| reqwest::get("https://api.company.com"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

For visibility on when operations fail and are retried, a `log::trace` message is emitted,
logging the `Debug` display of the error and the delay before the next attempt.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-features)wasm features

`again` supports [WebAssembly](https://webassembly.org/) targets i.e. `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which should make this
crate a good fit for most environments

Two cargo features exist to support various wasm runtimes: `wasm-bindgen` and `stdweb`.
To enable them add the following to your `Cargo.toml` file.

```
[dependencies]
again = { version = "xxx", features = ["wasm-bindgen"] }
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Retry](https://docs.rs/struct.RetryPolicy.html)- Policy
- A template for configuring retry behavior

# log 0.4.33 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log/^0.4

# log

A Rust library providing a lightweight logging *facade*.

A logging facade provides a single logging API that abstracts over the actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

## Minimum supported `rustc`

See the `rust-version` field in `Cargo.toml` for the current minimum Rust toolchain version.

This version is explicitly tested in CI and may be bumped in any release as needed. Maintaining compatibility with older compilers is a priority though, so the bar for bumping the minimum supported version is set very high. Any changes to the supported minimum version will be called out in the release notes.

## Usage

### In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided macros to
log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
```
use ;
```
### In executables

In order to produce log output, executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some options:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct [an FFI-safe wrapper over](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/421)to initialize in your libraries.`log`

- You may need to construct
- Utilities:

Executables should choose a logger implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logger implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the logger is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

## Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature, you can associate structured data with your log records:

```
use ;
```
